title: Callum's Splattery Science Surprise
markdown:
Dawn broke. Brilliant sunlight burst through the windowpanes, practically tickling Callum awake. Bright messy hair like a halo of pure energy as he bounced out of bed. Today was the day! The travelling science show was coming to the town square, and Callum, the town’s best gadget fixer, had a special job. He needed to show everyone the amazing differences between solids, liquids, and gases. He’d spent ages polishing gadgets, plugging in wires, and making sure his big bubbly contraption worked perfectly.

“Time to get ready!” His voice bounced. “Why some things stand tall, and others tumble and spill.” Tools clinked. Wires taut. Feet tap-tapped, eager for the square.

Mrs. Rowan bustled among chairs, spectacles on her nose, a gentle smile. High in an oak, Birch the squirrel perched, tail a bushy exclamation, nose twitching. Crowd-hum. Callum beamed like a polished bolt and tapped the microphone.

“Welcome! Super-duper building blocks of our whole world!”

He flipped a shiny switch. The machine did not gently demonstrate. It sputtered. Small colourful balls, meant to be solids, shot like confetti. Bright blue goo, meant to be liquid, splattered wide. Glittery gas, meant to stay put, erupted like a tiny volcano and dusted Mrs. Rowan’s spectacles, coating her nose in sparkles.

“Snapdragon sprouts!” Berry-red cheeks. The crowd ooohed. Birch chittered, blue goo dripping, surprisingly sparkly, from his tiny nose. Mrs. Rowan, sugary-donut dusted, blinked. “Whatever is happening?” The science show was a splattery disaster.

Birch, startled, tumbled from his perch. Thump, near spilled goo and scattered balls. He tried to scurry; paws slipped on the gloopy mess. He nudged a loose red ball. It stayed put. He pushed a dollop of blue goo. It spread, a slow-motion wave toward a dropped cookie.

“Look!” A sticky paw. “The little red balls don’t move! The blue sticky stuff just goes everywhere!”

Some things stay. Some things spread. Some things fill the air.

Callum knelt, flustered mind whirring, and watched. Balls kept their shapes. Goo flowed, taking the ground’s shape. The glittery gas had already gone everywhere, sparkle in the air.

“That’s it. That’s exactly it.” He held up balls. “Solids. Tiny bits — particles — packed tight. They cannot move around much, so they keep their shape. Like this pebble.” The grey stone by his foot had not joined the chaos.

A finger in the goo. “Liquid. Particles still close, but they slide past each other. That is why it spreads, like water finding a puddle.” A nod at the fountain. “And gas — the air we breathe, that glittery puff — particles zipping, far apart, filling any space they can.”

He quickly gathered more colourful balls and a cup of plain water, energy infectious again now that the lesson had arrived through a squirrel’s paws. He demonstrated: the balls stayed neatly themselves, not budging. The water spread in a wide happy puddle. He even blew a tiny puff of air at a fallen leaf, showing how a gas, even air, could push and move things. The crowd murmured with understanding, faces alight. They finally had the building blocks, even if the building had exploded first.

“Thank you, Callum,” Mrs. Rowan said, wiping glitter with a happy sigh. “And thank you, Birch, for showing us the way.”

Birch puffed his chest.

Callum did not declare the day AMAZING. He named the three behaviours once more, because a splattery lesson deserves clean words: packed and still; sliding and spreading; zipping and filling. Some things stay. Some things spread. Some things fill the air. Mrs. Rowan passed him a cloth. Birch washed his nose on the oak’s bark. The contraption, humbled, dripped one last polite sparkle, and Callum, who fixed gadgets for a living, began with the switch that should have been gentler, which is also a kind of science.
